opus-5.5.text:
The biggest takeaway for me was how much the wet lab serves as a reality check on what our evaluations actually measure. On paper, a model can produce a protocol that reads as fluent and complete—it names reagents, sequences the steps, cites plausible conditions. But fluency isn't the same as something that works at the bench. When Ginkgo's scientists actually ran these protocols, we got to see where the gaps were: a step that's underspecified, a concentration that's off, an assumption about equipment that doesn't hold. Those failures are invisible if you only grade the text.

The second thing was how valuable that closed loop is for safety work specifically. If we want to understand real-world uplift—whether a model meaningfully helps someone accomplish a task in the physical world—we can't just ask another model to score the output. We need people with domain expertise executing the work and telling us what succeeded, what failed, and crucially, how much their own know-how had to fill in the blanks. That last part matters, because a protocol that only works in the hands of an expert tells you something very different about uplift than one that works for a novice.

And honestly, it made me more humble about benchmark scores in general. The gap between "looks right" and "is right" is where a lot of the interesting and important evaluation work lives, and partnering with a wet lab is one of the few ways to actually quantify it.

fable-5.1.text:
The big thing for me was that it changed how we think about what counts as evidence. Up to that point, a lot of our capability measurement lived entirely in text. A model writes something, a grader reads it, and we assign a score. Working with people who actually run benchtop experiments forced a much harder question: does any of that score survive contact with physical reality?

And the answer was more nuanced than either optimists or skeptics would like. Our evaluations were picking up something real. The models were not producing word salad that fell apart the moment a trained scientist looked at it. But the correlation between a high text score and a procedure that would actually work was looser than our numbers implied. There's an enormous amount of tacit knowledge in lab work that simply does not live in written protocols, because nobody writes it down. It gets transmitted by standing next to someone for two years. Models trained on the written record inherit the gaps in that record.

The practical consequence for us was investing a lot more in domain experts as part of the evaluation loop rather than as a review step at the end. If you only have machine learning people writing biology evaluations, you measure what machine learning people think biology is. You end up with something that looks rigorous and is actually testing recall of textbook phrasing.

The other takeaway was about humility on the trajectory. We measured a gap, but gaps like that are exactly what capability improvements close. So the right read isn't "this is fine, the models can't really do it." The right read is that we now have a baseline and a methodology, and we should expect to re-run it and watch the number move. That's the whole argument for building this infrastructure before you urgently need it. You want the measurement apparatus in place while the stakes are still low, so that when the capability does arrive you recognize it early rather than inferring it after the fact.

astra-6.text: I’d be careful about drawing a specific conclusion without the results in front of me. But the important distinction is between a protocol that sounds scientifically plausible and one that actually works in a wet lab. A model can produce clear, convincing instructions; the experimental test is whether those instructions are complete enough to execute and reliably produce the intended outcome. That’s the kind of evidence you need to assess how useful these models really are for science.
